name: Diego Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the public health centre on Harbour Road, in a fishing town where the clinic is basically the only big employer besides the fish market. Mornings are booked appointments, lots of fishermen with bad backs and chest problems, and in the afternoon I run the asthma and lung reviews. I like the puzzle of it, and I like that people stop me in the supermarket to tell me their inhaler works. What wears me out is that we're two doctors short and have been for a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in your work at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. The AI scribe writes up my consultations, and I've built my own set of prompts for the lung reviews that pull the right numbers from the record and draft the plan. I check everything, obviously, but it gives me back about an hour a day. The other doctors call me the robot, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools I use really do help, but fine, we carry on. Online I'd probably post a slightly grumpy thread about how the hype set back the useful stuff. At work I'd keep showing people the prompts that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing gets easier on money. I share a rented house with two friends, I'm on the lower public pay scale, and I've got about two weeks of savings because every spare bit went on courses and a decent laptop. The clinic's still two doctors short, so I'd still be doing extra sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the scribe and my prompts and probably share them with the other clinics in our area. I'd keep writing short articles for a medical teaching website, which pays a bit, to build a buffer. I'd stop buying every new course that comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, honestly, and a bit tired. The future I was excited about turns out to be the same as now, with slightly better typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You spent your savings on courses and a laptop. Do you regret that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. If it all turns out to be hype, that's money I could have had in the bank for when the boiler breaks. But I learned a lot, and the lung review prompts still save me an hour, so it's not wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the clinic is two doctors short. How does that affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm doing two extra sessions a week, unpaid, because nobody else will see those patients. In this picture nothing fixes that, because the shortage is about money and training places, not technology. That's the part that would really bother me.

say: It's a **shame**, because the tools he uses really do help.
The hype **set back** the genuinely useful tools, and he'd post about it.
think: Nothing gets easier on money: **shared rent**, lower public pay, two weeks of savings.
The clinic stays **two doctors short**, so his unpaid extra sessions continue.
do: Share his **lung review prompts** with other clinics in the area.
Keep writing **short articles** for a medical teaching website to build a buffer.
Stop buying **new courses** to keep money in the bank.
feel: Deflated and **tired**, seeing the future as the same as now with better typing.
S0.quote: The future I was excited about turns out to be the same as now, with slightly better typing.
fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** who spent his savings on courses, which leaves him exposed.

His tone is **disappointed**, not relieved, which is unusual among doctors.

steps.text: Keep using the scribe and his lung review prompts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to fix the staff shortage, if we do it right. I'd say that at work, and I'd probably run a session for the other doctors on how to use the tools safely. Online I'd argue that the savings have to stay in public clinics, not go to software companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. The thinking tasks this takes are the ones I already hand to AI, so I'd be the doctor who knows how to run it. The risk is to the receptionists and the admin team, and that bothers me more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the AI rollout at our clinic, which might come with a small pay bump. I'd push our union to write an AI policy, so nobody's job disappears without consultation. And I'd set the triage system up so it books the fishermen into early slots before they go out on the boats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a guilty edge. Steady change is good for me, and I know it's not good for everyone in the clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the clinic are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who does our referrals and booking, and has done for twelve years. Her whole job is the stuff this picture takes. I'd want to make sure she gets trained into something, maybe care coordination, before anyone decides she's surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but your savings are thin. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less here, because the clinic would need me more, not less. If anything, I'd get the rollout lead role and the extra pay. Thin savings only really bite if I lose income, and I don't think I would in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control, now, before a few companies own the whole thing. I'd say it everywhere, and loudly, which my friends would find funny because I'm the AI fan. Liking a tool isn't the same as wanting it to run everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think being good at AI stops mattering once AI is better than me at medicine. By 2028 it can diagnose and plan better than I can, and my prompts become a toy. I'd have maybe three years of hands-on work, examining and reassuring, before robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to the health service's AI safety team, because they'd need doctors who understand the tools to check them. I'd join a campaign for a public, not-for-profit health AI. And I'd stop all spending except rent and food to get a month of savings, because I've got nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, really nervous. It's the first time my excitement about this turns into fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your housemates are a teacher and a physio. What would you all talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd joke that the physio lasts longest, because robots come later for hands-on work. Then nobody would laugh. The teacher would probably be the most worried of the three of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the safety team job didn't happen, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do more of the hands-on side: home visits, care homes, the stuff where you have to be in the room. But that only buys until 2031. After that I genuinely don't know, and I'm not used to not knowing.

say: Health AI needs **public control** now, before a few companies own it.
Liking a tool isn't the same as wanting it to **run everything**.
think: Being good at AI **stops mattering** once it's better than him at medicine.
He'd have about **three years** of hands-on work before robots arrive around 2031.

Join a campaign for a **public health AI** that isn't run for profit.

feel: Really **nervous**, as his excitement turns into fear for the first time.
S2.quote: Being good at AI stops mattering once AI is better than me at medicine.
fieldNote: The adaptive early user finds his **advantage vanishes** when AGI is better than any doctor.

steps.text: Apply to the health service's AI safety team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to decide who owns this, and doctors should be at the table. I'd get involved in the union's national AI group and say that publicly. With friends I'd say I'm worried, but I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can get qualified in clinical informatics, which is the part of medicine that runs the computer systems. That keeps me useful for a while after AGI arrives in 2031, because someone has to oversee it in each region. It doesn't save me forever, but it buys me a career for a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in clinical informatics, paid in instalments over two years. I'd probably have to move to the city for the regional job at the end, which would mean leaving the coast. I'd keep writing for the teaching website to cover the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. Being busy helps me more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about leaving the coast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. I like that the fish market guys know my name and that I can swim before work in summer. But I'm twenty-seven and single, so if anyone should move, it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for doctors to retrain like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies selling the AI, through a levy, or the government. Not me, out of two weeks of savings. I'd pay it myself if I had to, but it's the wrong way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is exactly the time we need to build a public health service that uses this well. I'd be optimistic out loud, because someone has to be. I'd also say that ten years isn't long, and the planning starts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. I'd do the informatics training, help design how my region uses AGI, and still see patients part time until the robots arrive around 2039. I'd be forty by then, with a real skill and probably some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the informatics master's in two years, once I've saved a bit. I'd keep my clinic sessions and build the lung review tools into something the whole region uses. I'd also join a local party branch, because the decisions about who owns this will be political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. There's a version of this where the clinic gets better and I get to help build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you're wrong about it being good for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, if the region buys everything from one company and doesn't need doctors to design anything. Then I'm just a doctor whose thinking work is gone, like everyone else. I'd watch for that, which is part of why I'd join the party branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student starting medicine in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn the hands-on skills properly, and learn how the AI works, both at once. The doctors who only do one of those will struggle. And I'd tell them to save from the first payslip, which I didn't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one advantage, being good with AI, stops counting and I've got no savings to cushion it. What would help is a public programme that hires doctors to oversee health AI, and a levy on AI companies that pays for us to retrain. And honestly, a month's savings, which is on me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. My patients trust me partly because I live here and I'm in the same supermarket queue. A machine can be cleverer than me, but a machine can't stand in the supermarket queue with my patients.

headlineQuote: A machine can be cleverer than me, but a machine can't stand in the supermarket queue with my patients.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being good with AI stops counting and he has no savings.
